chunks: "I think of it as building the inside first and the outside last. A fab starts with copper-clad laminate, which is fiberglass-epoxy with copper foil on both sides.
For a multilayer board they image and etch the inner layers first: coat with photoresist, expose the pattern with UV, develop, etch away the unprotected copper, strip the resist.
Then they inspect those layers optically, because after lamination you can't fix them.
Next the layers are stacked with prepreg between them and pressed under heat and pressure so it melts, flows and cures into one solid board.

Then they drill the holes, mechanically for normal vias and by laser for microvias, clean the resin smear out of the holes, and deposit a thin conductive layer so the barrels can be electroplated with copper.
After that the outer layers get imaged and plated, then etched.
Solder mask goes on next, as a green epoxy that leaves only the pads open, then silkscreen, then a surface finish like ENIG or HASL on the exposed copper.
Finally the boards are routed or scored out of the panel and electrically tested for opens and shorts. For me the point of knowing this is design rules.
Minimum trace/space comes from etching, minimum via size and aspect ratio come from drilling and plating, and that's what drives cost."
